Adam Stenavich.blurb: Stenavich ran a fairly conventional offense in Green Bay — middle of the pack on pass tendency, motion, screens, and tempo — but leaned meaningfully on RPOs, which ranked 13th, and the results were strong: 14th in offensive EPA/play across his four seasons calling plays. Andy Reid.blurb: Reid's offense throws the ball at one of the highest rates in the league and layers in elite RPO usage and a heavy screen game to keep defenses from teeing off on the pass — it's a varied attack that generates real results, sitting 13th in EPA/play. The nuance is that the system itself grades out middle of the pack once you adjust for quarterback and opponent, which means Mahomes is doing a lot of the heavy lifting. That's not a knock on Reid, but it's an honest read of where the scheme value actually sits.

Ben Johnson.blurb: Ben Johnson's offense doesn't win on exotic design — it wins on execution and structure. His scheme grades out fourth in system value across 76 play-callers, with a top-10 EPA/play to back it up, built on heavy play-action usage and a tempo that keeps defenses from settling. The profile is disciplined and balanced: middle-of-the-pack in pass tendency, motion, and creativity, which suggests the edge comes from how well the pieces fit together, not from trying to outscheme anyone.

Brian Schottenheimer.blurb: Schottenheimer's Dallas offense doesn't stand out on any single dimension — pass tendency, motion, play-action, tempo all land in the middle third — but the adjusted scheme value ranks seventh overall, which means the system itself is generating real worth beyond what the quarterback and matchups explain. That's the number that matters here. The results (EPA/play, also mid-pack) track with an offense built on execution rather than exoticness, and that's not a criticism.

Drew Petzing.blurb: Petzing runs a conventional offense by design — low in pre-snap exoticness, middle of the pack across nearly every schematic lever — and the results land right there too, with EPA/play and scheme value both sitting around the league median. That kind of profile can read as a knock, but it's worth noting that Detroit's offense has stayed functional without leaning on any single gimmick. The honest read: he's executing a straightforward system adequately, not elevating it.

Jim Bob Cooter.blurb: Cooter's Indianapolis offense leaned on play-action and RPOs more than most — top-15 in both — while staying conventional everywhere else. The results landed in the middle of the pack on EPA/play, which is about what a scheme built around those two constraints tends to produce without elite quarterback play to leverage them. He's now an OC who doesn't call plays, which is its own data point.

Kellen Moore.blurb: Moore's Saints offense sits squarely in the middle of the pack across nearly every measurable dimension — structure, tempo, tendency, and results. That kind of across-the-board averageness isn't inherently damning, but it does mean the scheme value (#23) is outrunning the actual production (#46 in EPA/play), which suggests the system is doing more work than the execution. Four seasons in, there's not yet a clear signature to point to.

Kevin O'Connell.blurb: O'Connell runs a fairly conventional offense — middle of the pack in structure, tempo, and most usage rates — with one real signature: he leans on play-action at a top-10 clip, which fits the identity he's built around his backfield. Kyle Shanahan.blurb: Kyle Shanahan's offense doesn't stand out as exotic or pass-heavy, but it produces like almost nothing else in the league — second in scheme value, fourth in EPA/play over this stretch. Everything else sits near league average, which is the point: the edge comes from structure and execution, not volume or trickery.

Matt LaFleur.blurb: Matt LaFleur runs one of the most valuable offensive systems in the league — third out of 76 coaches in QB- and opponent-adjusted scheme value — without leaning heavily on any single stylistic lever. The results back it up: top-15 in EPA/play. This is a system that wins on structure and execution, not novelty.

Matt Nagy.blurb: Nagy's offense in New York leans heavily on the pass and runs one of the highest RPO rates in the league, which gives it a clear identity even if the overall scheme value sits in the middle third. Mike LaFleur.blurb: LaFleur's Arizona offense is built on pre-snap motion — ranking 9th in the index there — while staying conventionally structured everywhere else: middle of the pack in pass tendency, play-action, tempo, and screens, with almost no RPO usage. Mike McDaniel.blurb: McDaniel runs one of the more structurally unusual offenses in the league — elite pre-snap motion, heavy screen usage, and a run-leaning tendency that puts him near the bottom in pass rate — but the results have settled in the middle of the pack on both scheme value and EPA. Sean McVay.blurb: McVay's offense isn't built on exotic concepts — it runs on pre-snap motion and play-action at rates that rank among the league's best, and the scheme itself grades out as genuinely valuable independent of who's running it. A disciplined, structure-first system that wins through preparation more than unpredictability.

Sean Payton.blurb: Sean Payton runs a varied, toolbox-heavy offense — high RPO usage, frequent screens, and genuine play-design creativity — but the results so far in Denver have been middling across the board. Some of that is quarterback, some of it is execution, but the output is what it is.

Shane Steichen.blurb: Steichen runs a balanced, RPO-heavy offense that doesn't lean on any single stylistic lever — the play-action, motion, and tempo numbers are all roughly league-average — but the scheme itself grades out well above the middle, ranking ninth in QB- and opponent-adjusted value. Todd Monken.blurb: Monken runs a remarkably balanced offense — every tracked tendency sits near the middle of the pack — yet the scheme still grades out as a top-10 system by value, which says the edge comes from execution and design quality rather than from trying to out-exotic anyone. This is a system built on doing the ordinary things well, and the data suggests that's genuinely working in Cleveland.

Zac Taylor.blurb: Taylor runs one of the most pass-heavy offenses in the league — top-4 in pass rate over expected — but the scheme itself is straightforward, ranking near the bottom in creativity. Brad Idzik.blurb: Brad Idzik runs a balanced, conventional offense in Carolina — nothing exotic, nothing particularly deliberate either, just a system that sits comfortably in the middle of nearly every measurable dimension. Liam Coen.blurb: Coen's offense doesn't lean on any one tendency — pass rate, motion, tempo, play-action all sit near the middle of the league — but the results are hard to argue with: top-five in both scheme value and EPA/play across his three seasons. Two seasons in, the results back the construction.

Worth noting he's currently in an OC role without play-calling duties, so the production here reflects his previous work as the caller.

Klayton Adams.blurb: Adams runs a conventional, low-decoration offense in Dallas — nothing exotic in the play design, minimal screen usage, middling motion and tempo across the board. He's no longer calling plays, so how much of that production travels with him is a real question.

Kliff Kingsbury.blurb: Kingsbury's Washington offense ranks in the top 4 in both RPO rate and play-action, which gives it an unusual structural range — defenses can't settle into a single read. Pass tendency is middling, meaning the run threat is real enough to make all of it work.

The speed is real, the scheme value isn't there yet, and two seasons in, the gap between tempo and production is the honest story.

Nick Caley.blurb: Nick Caley runs a conventional offense by almost every measure — middle of the pack in motion, tempo, play-action, and pass tendency — with the one notable outlier being a low screen rate. There's nothing here that's hurting Houston, but nothing that's creating structural advantages either.

Nick Holz.blurb: Holz runs a ground-heavy offense in Tennessee — low pass tendency, middling motion and play-action, nothing that stands out structurally — and the results reflect it. The execution isn't there, and the scheme isn't covering for it.

Whether that changes depends heavily on what Caleb Williams becomes.

Tim Kelly.blurb: Kelly runs a run-heavy, play-action-forward offense that moves fast and leans hard on screens to create easy completions — the overall shape is less about exotic concepts than about pace and structure. It's a coherent identity, just not one that's generating an edge over what the personnel would predict.

Tommy Rees.blurb: Rees runs a conventional, run-heavy offense in Atlanta — low pass rate, low RPO usage, deliberate tempo, nothing that jumps off the page schematically. Middle-of-the-pack scheme value with bottom-tier outputs is a difficult combination to defend after two seasons.

What's notable is that the results landed in the middle of the pack despite one of the least elaborate play-calling profiles in the dataset.

Brian Angelichio.blurb: Angelichio runs a stripped-down passing offense — high pass rate, almost no play-action, minimal motion, few screens or RPOs, and a deliberate pace — and the profile is consistent enough that you can call it a real identity rather than just a absence of features.
